title: Conduct Incident Management
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 7: Security Operations: Conduct Incident Management.

blocks.text: The CISSP Security Operations domain defines incident management steps as:

items: Detection — identify that an incident has occurred
Response — initial response to contain and assess the incident
Mitigation — actions to limit the impact of the incident
Reporting — notify stakeholders, management, and authorities as required
Recovery — restore systems to normal operations
Remediation — address the root cause to prevent recurrence
Lessons learned — post-incident review to improve processes

blocks.text: It's important to stress that incident management does not include just technical response — it encompasses the entire lifecycle from detection through lessons learned. The NIST SP 800-61 framework contains many of the same elements and has the same goal of effectively managing incident response. Each step is critical:

items: Detection: May come from automated systems (IDS/IPS, SIEM, AV alerts) or human observation (help desk calls, user reports). The ability to quickly and accurately detect incidents reduces their impact.
Response: The first response is to limit or contain the damage. This may include isolating affected systems, disabling compromised accounts, or blocking malicious IP addresses.
Mitigation: Goes beyond initial containment to actively reduce the impact. This may be ongoing as incidents are dynamic.
Reporting: Legal requirements may mandate notification to regulators, law enforcement, and affected individuals. Internal reporting to management is also essential.
Recovery: Restore systems from backups, rebuild from images, verify clean systems before returning to production.
Remediation: Address root cause — e.g., patching the vulnerability that was exploited, implementing anti-phishing training if the attack vector was phishing.
Lessons Learned: Formal post-incident review to identify what worked, what didn't, and what needs improvement.

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Know the CISSP-specific incident management steps in order: Detection → Response → Mitigation → Reporting → Recovery → Remediation → Lessons Learned. The NIST framework uses slightly different terminology but the concepts are the same.

items: Sources of detection: IDS/IPS alerts, SIEM correlation, antivirus alerts, user reports, audit log review, help desk tickets
Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) — artifacts that indicate a potential security incident has occurred
Importance of triage — quickly assess severity and scope to prioritize response efforts
Automated detection reduces mean time to detect (MTTD)
First priority: contain the damage and prevent further spread
Containment strategies: isolate affected systems/networks, disable compromised accounts, block malicious IPs/domains
Ensure response actions preserve evidence for potential investigation — maintain chain of custody
Activate the Incident Response Team (IRT) per the incident response plan
The IR team must identify both the current and likely future impacts of the incident
Actively reduce the scope and impact of the incident beyond initial containment
May involve: applying emergency patches, updating firewall rules, implementing additional monitoring
Details of the response effort need to be carefully documented during mitigation
Use pre-established runbooks, checklists, or reaction guides — people in a crisis situation do not always make the best decisions, so planning ahead is crucial
Internal reporting — notify management, CISO, legal, HR, and affected business units
External reporting — may be required to: regulators, law enforcement, affected individuals, breach notification authorities
Breach notification laws vary by jurisdiction — understand applicable timelines and requirements
Document all reporting actions: who was notified, when, by whom, what was communicated
Restore systems to normal operations with verified clean state
Steps: restore from known-good backups, rebuild from hardened images, apply current patches
Verify system integrity before returning to production — scan for remaining compromise indicators
Update security controls based on lessons from the incident
May involve operations transfer to an alternative facility if the primary site is compromised
Remediation — address the root cause to prevent the same or similar incidents from recurring
Examples: robust user anti-phishing training, blocking known malicious email senders/domains, implementing email security tools
Lessons learned — formal post-incident review meeting involving all stakeholders
Document: what happened, how it was detected, what went well, what needs improvement, action items
Update incident response plan, playbooks, and training based on findings
Use results to improve detective and preventive measures
